facts.t: The First Amendment came within 17 months
facts.d: The Constitution commenced on 26 January 1950; the First Amendment was passed in June 1951 — by the Provisional Parliament, a body elected on a limited franchise that was never itself voted in by the people it was amending the Constitution for.

facts.t: Article 368 borrows from three constitutions at once
facts.d: The special-majority requirement echoes the United States, the role of the President echoes Ireland, and the state-ratification device echoes Australia. Very few single articles in the Constitution are such a visible confluence.

facts.t: Most amendments never touch the states
facts.d: Only federally sensitive provisions — the election of the President, the distribution of legislative powers, the representation of states in Parliament, Article 368 itself — need ratification by half the states. The overwhelming majority of India's amendments have been passed by Parliament alone.

bank.q: With reference to the procedure under Article 368, consider the following statements:
s: A Constitution Amendment Bill may be introduced in either House.
In case of a deadlock between the two Houses, a joint sitting may be summoned.
The President is bound to give assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong — there is no joint sitting for a Constitution Amendment Bill; the two Houses are equal and each must pass it by special majority separately.

bank.q: The power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is best described as:
o: Ordinary legislative power exercised under the Seventh Schedule
Constituent power exercised specially by Parliament
Executive power exercised with legislative concurrence
bank.e: Amending power is constituent power — exercised outside the legislative division of powers in the Seventh Schedule. This distinction is the hinge on which Shankari Prasad, Golak Nath and Kesavananda all turn.

bank.as: The Constitution places no explicit restriction on Parliament's power to amend it.
bank.rs: The Basic Structure Doctrine is a judicial creation rather than a textual limitation.
bank.e: Both statements are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion. The absence of a textual limit is a fact about the drafting; that the limit which now exists is judge-made is a consequence of that absence, not its cause.

bank.q: Arrange the stages of a Constitution Amendment Bill requiring state ratification in correct order:
items: Ratification by the legislatures of half the states
Special majority in each House separately
Introduction in either House by any member
bank.e: Introduction in either House by any member → special majority in each House → ratification by half the states by simple majority → Presidential assent, which after the 24th Amendment is compulsory.

bank.q: Which one of the following is NOT correct about amendments requiring state ratification?
o: They also require a special majority in Parliament
The state legislatures must ratify by special majority
Ratification by one-half of the states suffices
They concern federally sensitive, article-specific exceptions
bank.e: State ratification needs only a simple majority in the state legislature. Requiring a special majority in the states as well would make the federal provisions almost unamendable.

bank.q: Consider the following arguments for restricting Parliament's amending power:
s: It preserves a balance between flexibility and stability.
It is expressly mandated by Article 368 itself.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are valid arguments. Statement 3 is wrong — Article 368 mandates no such restriction; the restriction came from judicial review and the Basic Structure Doctrine.

bank.q: Amendments that require only a special majority, without state ratification, concern provisions that are:
bank.e: Provisions unitary in character need only a special majority. Federally sensitive provisions — those touching the Union–State balance — attract the additional ratification requirement.

bank.q: All of the following are recognised checks on the amending power EXCEPT:
o: The rule that the amending power cannot itself be enlarged
A referendum requirement for amendments touching Part III
bank.e: India has no referendum requirement for any amendment. The other three are real constraints — the last one, no enlargement of amending power, is what Minerva Mills enforced against Articles 368(4) and (5).

bank.q: A Constitution Amendment Bill may be introduced by:
o: Only a Minister, and only in the Lok Sabha
Only a Minister, in either House
Any member, but only with prior Presidential recommendation
bank.e: Any member may introduce it in either House, and no prior Presidential recommendation is needed — unlike a Money Bill, which is confined to the Lok Sabha and requires recommendation.

bank.as: Article 368 is central to the debate between parliamentary sovereignty and constitutional supremacy.
bank.rs: The extent to which a constitution can be amended determines whether the legislature or the document is ultimately supreme.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion. An unlimited amending power makes Parliament sovereign; a limited one makes the Constitution supreme. India, through judicial intervention, chose the second.

bank.q: Consider the following statements about constituent power in India:
s: It is exercised by Parliament acting under the legislative entries of the Seventh Schedule.
It is held by Parliament in trust for the people.
It can be enlarged by an amendment made under Article 368 itself.
bank.e: Only statement 2 is correct. Constituent power sits outside the Seventh Schedule, and it cannot be enlarged by its own exercise — the attempt to do so through Articles 368(4) and (5) was struck down in Minerva Mills.
